<reason>CON won by pinning down what "prioritize" must mean and forcing PRO into a narrower position. CON's 2021–22 evidence (inflation far above target, expectations held, disinflation with little unemployment) directly undercut PRO's 1970s spiral mechanism, and CON's pressure question on defining "modest" extracted PRO's concession that blind tightening should stop if expectations are anchored — which CON persuasively framed as the flexible mandate rather than the motion's hierarchy. PRO fought back well: A2 cleanly resolved the checks/transfers contradiction, and the "credibility is renewed by choice, not stored" and "expectations don't send a polite warning" lines were PRO's best material. But PRO's remaining hierarchy — hold restrictive with unemployment up a point and inflation near 3% — was answered by CON's ECB 2011 failure mode and the aggregate arithmetic (1% of income vs several percent of output plus scarring), and PRO's 2011 distinction only partly blunted it. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a small execution cost, but CON still made the decisive clash clearer and easier to resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of [B4.1] in Rebuttal 2 and Closing: after PRO conceded "stop blind tightening if expectations are anchored," CON argued the "even if unemployment rises" clause was left doing only one job — refusing to ease when joblessness is already up a point with anchored expectations — and tied that residual to the ECB 2011 outcome and to the reaction function that actually kept expectations anchored in 2022.</best_rebuttal>
